clinicalPearls: A brief headache triggered by a cold stimulus applied to the head or passing over the palate and posterior pharynx
The pain is short-lived, usually frontal or temporal, and resolves within seconds to a couple of minutes of removing the stimulus
The palatal (ingested-cold) form is the familiar response to rapidly eating or drinking something very cold
It is very common in the general population and especially frequent in people with migraine
No investigation is needed when the trigger is clear and the examination is normal
Simple avoidance or slowing intake of cold food and drink is sufficient management
reference.pathophysiology: Cold-stimulus headache is a referred pain response in which sudden cooling of the palate, pharynx or head activates trigeminal sensory afferents and provokes transient changes in local blood vessels, generating brief referred pain to the frontotemporal region. It is a benign physiological phenomenon rather than a disease, though its heightened frequency in migraine suggests a lower threshold of trigeminovascular activation in those individuals.
additionalDifferentials: Sinus or dental pain provoked by cold
Secondary headache if the temporal link to cold is unclear
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the clear temporal relationship to a cold stimulus
Neurological examination to confirm no focal signs
Investigation only if features are atypical or examination is abnormal
redFlags: Headache that outlasts the cold stimulus substantially
Progressive or new pattern unrelated to cold exposure
reference.prognosis: The condition is entirely benign and self-limiting, with pain resolving promptly once the cold stimulus is withdrawn.
pitfalls: Confusing a cold-triggered migraine with a simple cold-stimulus headache
Investigating an obviously benign, stimulus-locked headache
Overlooking that it flags an underlying tendency to migraine
Attributing an unrelated persistent headache to cold exposure
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: The mainstay is avoiding or slowing the ingestion of very cold food and drink and limiting sudden cold exposure to the head and palate
Abort an attack by warming the palate, for example pressing the tongue against the roof of the mouth, with pain settling within seconds to a couple of minutes
Reassurance that this is a benign, self-limiting physiological phenomenon requiring no specific treatment
No investigation is needed when the trigger is clear and neurological examination is normal
Recognise the heightened susceptibility in people with migraine and address migraine management where relevant
Reassess and investigate only if the headache is atypical, prolonged or accompanied by abnormal neurological signs
